newsitem.title: CHINA: China plenum moves to tighten ideological control.
newsitem.headline: China plenum moves to tighten ideological control.

text.p: China's ruling Communist Party closed its annual policy-making plenum on Thursday by passing a decision to boost orthodox socialist values and signalling a tightening of ideological controls.

The plenum, which opened on Monday, also announced it had decided to hold its next congress, the party's 15th such meeting, in late 1997. Political upheavals and power struggles have forced changes in congress dates in the past.

"The congress is a meeting of great significance to be held at an important period during which China's reform and opening-up and socialist modernisation construction will be carried forward and forge ahead into the future," the Xinhua news agency quoted a plenum communique as saying.

"It will be a historic meeting for the CPC (Communist Party of China) to lead the Chinese people... to advance, in an all-round way, the great cause of building socialism with Chinese characteristics into the new century," it said.
The brief statement underlined the commitment of the ruling Communist Party to pushing ahead with the market-oriented economic reforms launched by paramount leader Deng Xiaoping in 1979.
However, the meeting appeared to adopt a tough line on ideology with language that harked back to the days when China's communist rulers paid more heed to orthodox Marxist ideas.
"The plenary session mainly discussed issues concerning ideological, ethical and cultural progress," Xinhua said.
The ruling party elite had gathered behind closed doors for their annual opportunity to set policy for the next year and to jockey for power and position, Chinese sources said.

Security was tight, with additional police on duty, around the site of the meeting in the Jingxi Guesthouse at the western end of Changan Avenue, or the Avenue of Eternal Peace, that cuts through central Beijing.

There was no immediate announcement of personnel changes in the top echelons of the Politburo, China's most powerful decision-making body, or other party organisations. Chinese sources had said changes in top jobs were unlikely at this meeting.

Diplomats said a reshuffle was unlikely because this could upset the current delicate balance of power and alliances in the party central committee and Politburo as jockeying for position begins in the run-up to the crucial party congress late next year.

Jiang had been expected to seize on the plenum as the last chance before the congress to underline his role as anointed heir to paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who has not been seen in public for more than two years and is fading gradually from the scene, diplomats and Chinese sources said.

Almost two decades of market-oriented economic reform have eroded what Beijing's top leaders regard as orthodox Marxist values, and party chief Jiang has made clear that he wants to place his stamp on ideology in China.
The party mouthpiece, the People's Daily, has filled its front-page for several days with examples of model workers and heroes, whom the populace at large should strive to emulate.
Among these was Beijing bus conductress Li Shuli, who is said to rise at 4 a.m. to make sure she is familiar with major sites along the route so she can help disoriented passengers.
Diplomats said Jiang was using the campaign -- coupled with a tough line on the media and ideology -- to boost his position.
